reviews.title: Make a difference not just money.
reviews.text: CEO's can learn so much from this book. Rewards for building a great company will come to founders and all stakeholders over time.

reviews.title: A toolkit to keep your company focused on its North Star
reviews.text: Eric has been on an incredible journey of both building companies and helping founders. He's lived the problems that he chooses to train his attention on — they're real, important problems and he comes with pragmatic and actionable solutions. Having a toolkit for ensuring that a company doesn't go off mission is perhaps one of the most important things a founder can have. I highly recommend this.

reviews.title: Essential reading for any aspiring founder
reviews.text:
This is one of the best books I have read recently, and I can't recommend it enough. I spent the last months trying to figure out how to build a company that is mission-protected. I read a number of books and articles, but none hit the mark like Incorruptible. Eric Ries was able to put into word many concepts I thought about but didn't really know how to articulate. I particularly loved the examples: now, when I talk to other founders or investors about steward ownership and the perils of short-term profit maximization, I have so many clear examples to share that bring the concepts to life.

I think every aspiring entrepreneur should read this book. It is clear that building a startup is not just about shipping an MVP out fast, but founders should think early also about how to build in a way that protects the company and their work in the long term, and that allows a company to survive and thrive in the long term.

I finished the book inspired, with clear frameworks on how to implement a mission-lock in real life, and hopeful that I have finally found a community of people who share my same vision for businesses and a new type of capitalism.
reviews.note: Same reviewer as Goodreads user Federica (4 textReviews — under quantitative bar)

reviews.title: The question is not only how we align models, but who aligns the companies aligning them
reviews.text: Eric Ries' *Incorruptible* is a sharp reminder that companies are not ruined only by bad people, but by bad structures. A mission statement means little if the business model quietly defeats the mission. Costco's $1.50 hot dog and Kirkland quality, Apple's care for the inside of a computer most users would never see, and Anthropic's long-term benefit trust all point to the same principle: trust must be engineered before growth attracts predators. This is especially urgent in AI. The question is not only how we align models, but who aligns the companies aligning them. Public benefit charters, mission guardians, director duties tied to purpose, and better measurement can help close the distance between customers, executives, and the public interest. In the end, incorruptibility is not idealism. It is durable design.

reviews.title: A textbook for startup founders to ensure their survival in the company they are creating
reviews.text:
Who would have imagined 15 years ago that the author who was immersed in the popular "chase the money" phase of the startup world would continue and gather so much insight into the failures of just chasing the money?
Books like "In Search of Excellence" and "Good to Great" have not aged well, with the companies selected based on financial performance over a few years.
On the positive side, a few other writers in past years have researched the traits of companies that survive wars, depressions, and technological change and live for 100 years or more - Arie de Geus - "The Living Company". And another looking at the long-term financial results of companies that have ethical behaviors at their core - Sisodia, Sheth, Wolfe - "Firms of Endearment". These and other writers have observed the importance of purpose and ethics in business, but what is missing is how to counter predatory rent-seeking by people focused on maximizing what they can extract in the short term, even at the expense of the company. Eric Ries closes this critical gap.

reviews.title: Transformational business book
reviews.text: Transformational book on how leaders can contextualize work and its connections to purpose. Great depth of background research and thought.

reviews.title: from the bathroom floor
reviews.text:
You will run into memorable stories and statements right from the start. I couldn't put this book down until done; and if you are serious about business success, you might experience that too! The premise is simple and Eric says it so well;

"Over the weeks that followed, The Professor and I forged a different path for his fledgling company. A path that would allow them to shape their own future. Discovering that path required me to unlearn everything I thought I knew about business, from the very definition of profit itself to the fundamental way we build and structure organizations. Now let me share it with you."

reviews.title: A must read!
reviews.text: A must read and a great addition to his other books that become the standard for startups and big companies alike. Eric takes both a high level view and a detailed look at the heart of companies and what really matters. The stories from Costco and others are fascinating. Highly recommend this book!

reviews.title: Mission isn't culture. It's structure.
reviews.text:
Started reading expecting another mission-and-values book. Two chapters in, I called my lawyer.

Ries does something I haven't seen in any other founder book: he reframes mission protection as a structural problem, not a cultural one. The argument is that culture drifts over time, but structure stays in place. That single distinction reorganized how I think about company building.

The chapter on financial gravity hit hardest. The idea that financial pressure actively pulls you toward shortcuts that compromise your mission, regardless of how aligned you think you are, named the failure mode I'd been most worried about but couldn't articulate. For any business built on trust, that's the slow leak that kills you before you notice.

The book is also unusually practical. The Incorruptible Blueprint lays out specific structural moves: encoded purpose in the certificate of incorporation, founder bridge voting, founder liquidity provisions, mission guardian relays. It's not a manifesto. It's a checklist.

Ries's advice for early founders is to do this work before financial gravity makes it harder. The window is wider than you think, but it closes.

I bought six copies for my cofounders and key engineers. That's how much I think this matters.

reviews.title: Guidebook for entrepreneurs who want to maintain mission-alignment
reviews.text:
As a mission-driven entrepreneur, I really appreciated this book.
The book does a great job of pairing idealistic aspirations with concrete, pragmatic advice for entrepreneurs on how to maintain control of their companies or how to keep the company aligned to its mission even after they leave. It includes a number of helpful case studies and anecdotes, along with actual corporate governance best practices that can make the difference between maintaining or losing control of one's company. I think this book would be very useful both for social entrepreneurs who are idealistic and want to maintain fidelity to the mission, and also for a broader set of entrepreneurs who want to know what they have to do to maintain control of their company and avoid losing it as they raise and bring in more outside investors and stakeholders. The book has some interesting analysis of the incentives for lawyers, investors, and independent board members that can lead to entrepreneurs losing control of their company despite listening to all the people they're supposed to consult. I also think the book could be very useful for business school students to understand some of the deeper intricacies of corporate governance and mission-driven companies.

I've been a fan of Eric Ries since I first read "The Lean Startup," and this book does not disappoint!

reviews.title: As a founder: this book is a must read.
reviews.text:
I absolutely loved this book -- couldn't put it down.

Every days feels like a new company turning its back on its users and values -- a process Ries calls "Corruption," and it sometimes feels like that's the inevitable part of the lifecycle that companies are doomed to and users/customers are cursed with.

This book shows that no, it's a choice. It's chock full of case studies of companies who have avoided that fate, and has advice for those of us who want to as well. Narratives are interspersed with research and case studies going back decades (and sometimes centuries) of "mission-controlled" organizations who have resisted the siren song of short-term financialization and have thrived.

Be warned: the "Incorruptible Blueprint" challenges almost every piece of conventional wisdom that I was told and never quite believed, so following it may feel like swimming upstream. But it's a timely and refreshing reminder that encrapification is a choice not an inevitability, that there is a better way, and that you're not alone in trying to find it.

As a founder, this book was deeply hopeful. As a consumer, deeply cathartic. I hope everyone trying to build a company reads this and takes inspiration from it. I hope every funder does as well, and takes seriously all of the evidence that "incorruptible" companies statistically wildly outperform ones that fall prey to short-term tactics.

This one's going to be a classic.

reviews.title: The how-to to make companies do what you wish they did
reviews.text: I was able to read and review an earlier draft. This book is a necessary antidote to the usual "maximize profits at all costs" blind following. Most companies and people have goals that are not *only* short term profit maximizing, and Eric has detailed the ways that you can set up the legal and corporate structures so that the companies you create can actually align with those goals

reviews.title: Required reading before your next cap table conversation
reviews.text: I had the chance to read Incorruptible early, and it's the rare business book that earns the hype. Eric Ries does for company longevity what The Lean Startup did for company creation, but the argument here is sharper and, frankly, more uncomfortable. His thesis, that mission drift in successful companies is a structural problem rather than a moral one, reframes a debate most founders have been having backwards for years. Reading it as an operator building in AI, where everything from cap tables to incentive structures is forming under enormous time pressure, the timing felt almost personal. Incorruptible gives you the vocabulary and the blueprint to make governance decisions deliberately rather than by default, and it's the book I'll be handing to every founder I know.

reviews.title: Excellent audio book format as well!
reviews.text: I got the audiobook and loved that Eric read it himself! He's an amazing communicator and this book will inspire you to think about important, new ideas.

reviews.title: Transformational
reviews.text: A visionary look at the future of compassionate capitalism. A triumph

reviews.title: All investments have impacts ... Positive Impact Investing is the Goal
reviews.text:
Eric has a powerful way with words. In this book we have to open our eyes and ears to see a series of complex interaction of governance, power, and purpose. He dances us through multiple examples of how a narrow interpretation of the goal of corporation has driven companies, people and society to damaging outcomes.

With lots of illustrations, he shows positive and negative examples. Often showing how (and sometimes why) incoherence creeps in in the pursuit of profits. He has unearthed a treasure trove of structural methods that work to keep the mission in business.

Like me and others who believe that entrepreneur-lead innovation is exceptional at spotting and attacking pain points with persistence, Eric is an admirer the power of capitalism to drive innovation. Right now, in these unprecedented times, many people are discussing how to build a bridge between philanthropy and conscious capitalism to build system-level solutions that benefit the planet and support the people who will live on it. At my organization, LearnLaunch Fund + Accelerator, we invest in impactful companies that can move the needle on education and workforce upskilling.

Corruption does steal value from value creators - Eric has helped crystalize some seeds of hope. Jean Hammond

reviews.title: Essential reading for founders and board members
reviews.text:
I spent years in finance before becoming a founder, which means I've sat on both sides of the table where missions go to die. Ries calls that "financial gravity." It's the structural force that bends even well-intentioned companies toward extraction as they scale. He explains that this doesn't have to happen. It's simply bad design.

Instead of treating governance as a compliance checklist, Ries reframes this as creative work, a design opportunity. The decisions founders make about ownership, board structure, and charter are much more than compliance. They determine whether a company's mission survives its own success. Costco is a favorite case study, quietly proving for decades the power of choosing long-term stakeholder health over quarterly shareholder performance.

Every entrepreneur, founder, and board member should read Incorruptible. It's practical, insightful, and Ries gives you as much to do as he does to think about.

reviews.title: A new Eric Ries
reviews.text:
Eric evolution as a writer and a business person is incredible.
If you read his previous works, The Lean Startup, The Startup Way, The Leader's Guide, you may see the shift that he took towards a more holistic view on the modern world and how he is worried for our society.

This is definetely his turning point and I was so lucky to read this book early during its development.

reviews.text: I wish I had had this book when I started my company. This shows what mission-driven looks like in action when it is successful, what things you do and do not compromise on, and how to encode your values into systems that far outlast the founding team. Strong recommend for anyone interested in how to build a thriving company that stands the test of time.

reviews.title: Avoid the pitfalls that destroyed so many brilliant businesses!
reviews.text: This book delivers an accessible analysis of the pitfalls of modern business economics. Promising, ethical, even mission-driven businesses have been gutted by private equity, greed, and misplaced trust in bankers who stand to profit no matter what.

reviews.title: A roadmap for a different course
reviews.text: Eric Ries powerfully gives language to a dynamic that many of us have felt in our bones: how so many things, ideas, companies that start out beautiful and pure decay — corrupt — over time. More importantly, he offers a roadmap for entrepreneurs and leaders who hope to steer a different course.

reviews.title: A book that doesn't just inspire — it makes you stop and think.
reviews.text:
Eric Ries wrote The Lean Startup to help founders build something worth protecting. With Incorruptible, he's written the book he should have written next, because it turns out that knowing how to build is only half the battle. The harder question is how you keep what you've built from being quietly hollowed out.

The central argument is both simple and devastating: mission corruption isn't a moral failure. It's an engineering failure. "Financial gravity" - the doctrine of shareholder primacy is a force so deeply embedded in corporate law, investor expectations, and boardroom norms that it bends even the most principled founders toward extraction, often without anyone noticing until it's too late. 

What makes this book exceptional is that Eric doesn't stop at diagnosis. He is, above all, an engineer and he brings that same rigor here. The Sol Price story alone is enough to shake you up. Price built FedMart on the philosophy that a business exists to genuinely serve its members and was ousted from his own company by his own board, not because he failed, but because the structure couldn't protect the mission when financial gravity pulled hard enough. It's a haunting opener.

Eric also tells us how to protect the mission through solid well-researched examples. Costco's governance fortress. Patagonia's extraordinary restructuring that made the earth its majority shareholder. GitLab's invisible leader- values so embedded in operations that they guide decisions without anyone needing to be in the room. Novo Nordisk optimizing for patients and paradoxically becoming one of the most valuable companies on earth. Each case study is carefully chosen not to inspire envy but to prove a point: the harder-is-easier mission actually works. Genuine purpose, structurally protected and consistently acted upon, compounds.
reviews.note: Same review text as Sudha Shankar on Goodreads

reviews.title: An engaging deep study and set of tools for keeping organizations mission-aligned
reviews.text: Eric Ries was generous enough to share an advance copy, and even partway through, the thesis is clear: this is a playbook for building guardrails around good intentions. It takes on one of the hardest questions in organizational life: how do you keep purpose intact when growth, capital, and institutional momentum are all working against it? The governance frameworks here are concrete and tested, useful for founders designing their structures from scratch and for mature organizations needing a course correction. This is a exactly the kind of serious, practical thinking we need right now.

reviews.title: Now I know why some companies feel different
reviews.text: I'm not in business or startups, I'm just someone who shops, works, and pays attention. This book finally explained something I'd always felt but couldn't name: why a few companies seem to actually stand for something while most slowly let you down. Eric Ries calls the pull toward cutting corners "Financial Gravity," and shows how rare companies are built to resist it. I read it as a regular person and came away a sharper customer, voter, and employee.

reviews.title: Explains why I love Costco so much
reviews.text: I'm just an ordinary consumer, and this book rewired how I see every brand I buy from. Eric Ries shows why most companies drift toward cutting corners, and how a rare few are designed to stay true. Clear, honest, and genuinely eye-opening. No wonder I love Costco so much.

reviews.title: The defining guide for ethical organization-building
reviews.text:
In a world obsessed with growth at all costs, Incorruptible is the reality check we desperately need. Eric Ries shifts the conversation from merely "building fast" to "building right."

The book is packed with the signature analytical style Ries is known for, balanced with powerful real-world examples. It challenges readers to look closely at the systems they are creating and offers a blueprint for injecting true integrity into everyday business operations. It's a profound read that left me with a long list of notes and ideas to apply to my own work. Truly excellent.

reviews.title: Important for founders to pick up
reviews.text: Designed specifically for founders, it provides a lot of context and hidden depths you don't find elsewhere without a lot of work.

reviews.title: Eric's light shines on with Incorruptible (and it's brighter than before)
reviews.text:
The Lean Startup changed my life and the world of entrepreneurship 15 years ago, and seeing Eric let his light shine on the world once again with "Incorruptible" felt like a rallying cry.

This book seems like a natural maturation of his life's work: from teaching us how to build something great, to now showing us how to protect it from the corruption and short-term thinking that kills so many great companies.

A must-read for an founder, early-stage employee/operator, investor (private and public), and anyone hoping to reclaim capitalism as an additive force that propels humanity forward instead of the extractive, misguided, and dehumanizing form of savage capitalism that has corrupted our world's understanding of what "value" truly is.

reviews.title: Eric Ries's New Book Will Change How You Think About Building Companies
reviews.text:
Eric Ries spent fifteen years teaching founders how to build companies. The Lean Startup has become a sacred text for founders. His new book is even more important. The premise of Incorruptible is that the drift from idealism to extraction we keep watching in great companies isn't an ethical failure, it's a structural one. Founders sell out, boards prioritize short-term returns, missions erode - not because the people inside became bad, but because corporate architecture never gave them the conditions to stay good. Ries's answer is that enduring organizations are neither investor-controlled nor founder-controlled. They are mission-controlled. And he describes in wonderful detail how to achieve that.

The Lean Startup told you how to build something. Incorruptible tells you how to keep what you've built from corrupting itself once it starts working. That's a harder and, I'd argue, more important question. The problems we're working on in modern business are structural, not personal, and the answer requires re-engineering the institutions, not just exhorting the people inside them to be better. Truly a must-read!

reviews.reviewer_name: Ryan H (Ryan Honeyman, B Corp Handbook author)
reviews.title: Important for B Corps, Social Entrepreneurs, and Mission-Driven Leaders
reviews.text:
I am the author of "The B Corp Handbook." Incorruptible is one of the most important books for the B Corp movement I have ever read.

Eric's main point in the book is that good companies do not usually lose their way because people stop caring. They drift because "financial gravity" pulls their ownership, governance, incentives, investors, and accountability systems away from their stated purpose.

His warning for B Corps is especially important: benefit corporation status helps, but it is not enough.

Allbirds is a vivid example. The company was both a B Corp and a public benefit corporation, yet financial gravity pushed them to rapidly scale and overextend in search of profitability. Eventually, as we saw in recent news headlines, this pressure contributed to a dramatic unraveling of the company's original business model and mission identity. That does not mean B Corp certification or benefit corporation laws are meaningless. It means that B Corps need to get creative to ensure their long-term viability.

The companies Eric points to include well-known B Corps like Tony's Chocolonely and Patagonia, along with mainstream businesses like Anthropic, IKEA, Hershey's, Novo Nordisk, and Costco, all have unique mission-locked architecture. Whether through mission guardians, foundations, trusts, employee ownership, or otherwise, all of these companies are designed to resist pressure over time.

For B Corps, Incorruptible is a reminder that going beyond the standard "B Corp + benefit corp" structure is needed to build companies that are set up for the next 50 to 100 years or longer.

reviews.title: A must-read that will change how you build.
reviews.text: Incorruptible is an absolute game-changer and essential reading for any founder. Eric brilliantly shows how to build structural integrity directly into a company's design and this book gives me immense hope for the future of business. Highly recommended!

reviews.title: A new blueprint for long-term success
reviews.text:
Eric Ries brings the same clarity and systems thinking that made The Lean Startup so influential to one of the biggest questions facing anyone building or managing a company: How do we create organizations and businesses that last? The Lean Startup was all about starting and scaling business ideas; Incorruptible outlines the elements and processes required to protect scale and resilience over the long term. It sharpens the focus on what allows organizations to endure -- and on the forces that can quietly undermine them. A smart, practical, essential book.
Also: great bonus content in the audio edition.

reviews.title: A Must-Read: Eric Ries' Seminal New Book
reviews.text: This is a must read by anyone in the business world. Eric has written another seminal book. He recognizes that the problem is one of design, not character, identifying ownership, incentives, governance, and accountability as the variables that favor short-term capital over long-term purpose. Most founders are incorruptible, but the system fails them by not sufficiently binding a company's future leaders to the founders' original purpose and vision, contributing to a long-term dilution of the non-financial variety.

reviews.title: Important for leaders to know
reviews.text: In an economic age that seems plagued by grift, gambling, and speculation, Ries has a welcome message in this book: It's not enough to build a company that will make money; leaders should be thinking about how to create organizations that will endure and make positive contributions to the world.

reviews.title: Eric Ries has done it again!
reviews.text:
Incorruptible is an important and timely book about why even well-intentioned companies so often lose their way as they scale. Incorruptible is especially valuable because it does not reduce corporate failure to "bad people" or isolated ethical lapses. Ries focuses instead on the systems, incentives, governance structures, and financial pressures that gradually pull companies away from their original missions.

The book is thoughtful, practical, and clearly informed by Ries's deep experience with startups, founders, investors, and long-term company building. It is most useful for founders, CEOs, investors, board members, and anyone who cares about building organizations that can remain principled as they become successful.

Highly recommended for readers interested in entrepreneurship, governance, corporate culture, and the long-term consequences of how companies are designed.

reviews.title: A worthy sequel to The Lean Startup
reviews.text: Most books about why good companies go bad blame bad leaders or corrupt individuals. But the problem is deeper than that. I've been a fan of Eric Ries since The Lean Startup, which has influenced Silicon Valley and beyond for 15+ years. Now he's looking at a huge problem in society - corruption and malfeasance, which seems to be everywhere these days. His argument about the structural causes is powerful, because it means there are factors that can lure even 'good' companies and leaders to bad outcomes - but if we make the right changes, we can help prevent many problems upstream. A smart book from a deep thinker.

reviews.title: a Hearful business book that might just make you cry while giving you practical advice
reviews.text: This book is a MUST read for any founder, board member, investor, who actually wants to create a company that benefits humanity. This book had me sobbing at some of the stories, this book also gave me so much hope that there is another way.

reviews.title: A book every great builder should read
reviews.text: A book every great builder should read. From one of our all time great thinkers, Eric does an incredible job of making Incorruptible practical, insightful, and exciting to read. This is definitely a guide I'll be carrying forward throughout my career.

reviews.title: Provides the roadmap to build a company that outlasts you and benefits humanity
reviews.text:
This book basically took everything that we've been thinking about for our business and just expressed it in a way that we could feel and connect to it instantly. It's absolutely brilliant and very difficult to put down.

Thank you for giving us a roadmap for what to do ahead as we look to establish our business to outlast us and benefit humanity. We are forever grateful at OPERAScale.

reviews.title: Thought-Provoking!
reviews.text: "Incorruptible" is an engaging and insightful read that really makes you think about leadership, trust, and how systems can work better. Eric Ries does a great job blending big ideas with practical examples that feel relevant and easy to connect with.

reviews.title: Defining book for the next century.
reviews.text: Incorruptible is an essential book for the next century. Businesses are a huge part of all of our lives; Eric sheds a new light on how they work, why they work, and what we as a society deserve from them. It's also a practical and fun read, with everything from talking points for your lawyer to honestly the funniest set of chapter epigrams ever. It's a blast. You should read it.

reviews.title: Antidote
reviews.text: Highly recommended to anyone currently in business or thinking about it. Corporations don't have to be evil. The author manages to make corporate governance accessible with quick analogies and longer stories of businesses across history. Tell your coworkers to read this book.

reviews.title: The book title says it all, one of the most important books ever written
reviews.text: Read an early version of the book and have been exposed to Eric's ideas for years. This book is a guide for future leaders of the world, and I implore anyone looking to do business for the better to read it. Not next week, but today!

reviews.title: This is the pill you take when you want to vaccinate your company against greed.
reviews.text:
Companies go bad because they are obsessed with ensuring the last lines of their financial statements look good. That is often what is good for investors in the short term.
But they lose out on the long game, on the potential to build great products that solve great problems and ultimately hurt the soul of the company. Grab this book to think through how to protect your company from this progression.

reviews.title: Hold on to your ideals
reviews.text:
If you're a founder who doesn't want your company to be corrupted by bad incentives, read this book.

I'm a founder of a seed stage company who grew up on the Lean Startup. I've been a part of companies that used the lean startup method to find PMF and scale to $20m+ in revenue in under two years.

In every success story I've seen, the company loses it's culture and it's mission orientation, leading to some spectacular blowups and failures. This book provides compelling stories of companies that failed and succeeded to hold on to their ideals, and more importantly, a framework for how to protect your future company from losing sight of why this all matters.

reviews.title: A new playbook for startups. A must read for Founders
reviews.text: Any Founder, or people supporting them, needs to read this. Logical, actionable, and the obvious playbook for the future. It's mind boggling we made it this far without integrating the ideas Eric lays out into our standard best practices for the startup and venture world. Well done Eric!

reviews.title: A must read for every founder, ideally before taking investment!
reviews.text:
I just finished Incorruptible and it might be the most important book I have read as a mission-focused founder. It's one of those rare moments where I can point to exact paragraphs that will rewire how I spend the next thirty years of my life.

Here is some context on why it landed so hard. I was a intelligence/targeting officer in the Air Force and I watched missions fail and people die because of bad software. After a particularly bad incident, I got myself reassigned to software procurement where they built my terrible software and launched Kessel Run, the operating model for which I borrowed heavily from Lean Startup / Startup Way. It was wildly successful but the mission was corrupted by the enterprise. So I left and started Rise8 to help future rebels win that fight.

We're now in the Star Wars arc where the Empire Strikes Back (!), but I'm optimistic that we will win. My purpose is to make govtech work better, and I envision a future where fewer bad things happen because of bad software. We ship outcomes in govtech. That is a mission that cannot afford corruption, but it is unfortunately one of the most corrupt spaces in the country.

Until finishing this book, I genuinely believed there were only two paths. Path one: take investment, accept that gravity eventually wins, and watch whatever I built get hollowed out the moment I'm not in the room. Path two: take no outside capital, stay personally in control, move slower, and accept that the whole thing dies with me. I had quietly chosen path two and I told myself the tradeoff was the price of integrity.

This book made me realize I had been staring at a false dichotomy the entire time. It's possible to be "Incorruptible" and I've already gotten to work on it.

I'd love for there to be a companion book for government technologists and protecting innovative programs from corruption. This book has also given me ideas for that. It's an important mission--analog governments will not persist in a digital world. I believe things are falling apart politically because of the impedance mismatch between an analog government and a digital world. Rising populism, demagoguery, and extremism all stem from failing to deliver. Digital government isn't just a nice-to-have 'digital transformation' thing, it is existential.

I believe transforming government is possible, but I had growing anxiety that my current path wouldn't get there in time. Thank you for showing a better way.
reviews.note: Rise8 founder, Air Force vet, ex-Kessel Run — strong governance-in-govtech angle

reviews.title: Thinking about starting a company? Read this book before you do!!
reviews.text: If you have been thinking about how you can start a company without selling your soul to the financial devil, this is a book for you! Yes, it is possible. But you need to set yourself up for success from the beginning - you need to make sure that your mission is aligned with your founding documents, you need to make sure that your strategy and vision stay core to your mission. Great addition to his previous books. It's a readable book, with great examples. But read this early - before you have already set yourself on the path to being ruled by money only.

reviews.title: Engaging and Practical
reviews.text:
As a founder, as an employee, as a mission-driven leader, and as a human, I LOVE this book. Eric Ries caught my attention back in 2011 when he released his first book, The Lean Startup. The Lean Startup captured, named, and programatized product and market development tools that turned Silicon Valley on its ear and brought terms like "MVP" and "pivot" into the common parlance. The focus was on building something of _real_ value.

Fast forward fifteen years and the focus of Incorruptible is on _protecting_ that value. I have had a front row seat to the value destruction that takes place when unprotected visions are subject to the whims of the capital market. Valuable businesses are torn apart because the margin is too low for the acquiring company. Startups are starved for funding because their potential for return is just a bit too slow or a bit too low. Humans are severed from jobs they've dedicated themselves to for years so that a quarterly earnings call can be made (never mind how the company will continue creating value in the future with no staff).

In Incorruptible, Eric has established both a mindset and a concrete set of actions to take to ensure that your company can stay true to its vision and truly deliver the value that you set out to deliver. He rebuts the notion of common "best practices" that focus on extractive potential and short term gains and provides convincing evidence that "mission-locked" companies perform _significantly better_ on every metric than companies that allow their mission to drift in pursuit of money.

If you want to build a successful company (think Costco or Patagonia), that remains focused on its mission and literally cannot be broken by outside interference, you gotta read this book and implement its thesis.

reviews.title: A Book Every Leader Needs to Read!
reviews.text:
I will say this is the most important business book every leader can read right now!

The organizations we start are under constant pressure to change, and along the way, most lose sight of what their organization stood for and what mattered… It's time for something different!

reviews.title: The Case for Durable Corporate Design and Value Accretion
reviews.text:
For CEOs and board members focused on building enduring companies, Incorruptible is essential reading. The book tackles one of the defining challenges of modern governance: how companies preserve mission, integrity, and long-term strategic focus as they successfully scale and navigate public-market pressures.

What makes the book compelling is its case-study focus on governance, accountability, and leadership systems that support durable value creation over short-term optimization. It reinforces the important principle shared by many of the world's most respected long-term companies: great companies are not built quarter-to-quarter, but through intentional stewardship, aligned incentives, and a commitment to long-term value creation.

A timely and important contribution to the broader conversation around long-term capitalism, companies and sustainable leadership.

reviews.title: Inspiring book even if you aren't an aspiring entrepreneur
reviews.text: I don't typically read business books, but I made an exception and I am glad I did. Eric Ries is a gifted story teller. This is an entertaining and thoughtful book about how entrepreneurs can build successful businesses and contribute to a more resilient society.

reviews.title: What matters most about running a business
reviews.text: This book is a revolutionary roadmap about how to build and lead thriving, sustainable businesses. It reveals the hidden story behind what makes companies and their workforces flourish. And, it's a fascinating read!

reviews.title: The cure for encrapification is hiding in plain sight - a must-read
reviews.text:
This tour de force is both diagnosis and cure for encrapification — the inexorable decay of products, services, and companies from great to meh to RIP. While it's tempting to blame a lack of moral integrity, every autopsy reveals the same disease, the same corruption, the same black hole that consumes every company that follows the standard playbook. While these 'best practices' have been foisted upon founders and companies for the past 50 years, Eric shows that, in fact, they actually destroy value, as predictably as the day follows night and despite the best of intentions.

Fortunately, as Eric points out, these worst practices are optional and there is a FAR better path. Amazingly, even though it's the path less followed, it's well-trodden and leads to far greater success, by every measure. The path diverges early in the journey and advisors won't tell you about it, so this book is a must-read for anyone building or advising a company, and anyone wondering why their favorite brands, products, restaurants, etc. go from fab to bad.

reviews.title: Amazing read!
reviews.text: This is the book I wish I had when I founded my company. Eric provides not only real world examples from brands we all know but also breaks down a framework for founders to follow. Amazing read!
reviews.note: Possibly Leah Solivan, TaskRabbit founder — back-of-book endorser. Verify before crediting.

reviews.title: A hopeful page turner
reviews.text: Really enjoyed this book. We live in seemingly dark times, filled with corporate greed, corruption, and value misalignment. Incorruptible doesn't hide from these issues, but rather meets them head on, showing examples of how organizations can be built and maintained for the betterment of humanity. At its core this book is hopeful and it's filled with inspiring stories that make you keep turning pages. If you're looking for a manual that shows a new, positive path forward for companies in the age of crony capitalism, give Incorruptible a try.

reviews.title: A compelling argument for compassionate capitalism by a master founder and storyteller
reviews.text:
"Incorruptible destroys the myth that only sleazy founders and companies get rich. Eric Ries shows you how to build a mission-driven company that will be humane, ethical, and make piles of money for decades. And Eric's charm, wonderful writing, and warm wisdom make this book a rare joy to read."

Congrats to Eric Ries on the publication of his compelling and timely book. I read it and loved it, and had a blast interviewing Eric about at Manny's in San Francisco a few weeks back. He's so brilliant and a world-class story-teller.

I am honored to have my blurb on the back of the book. Above is the original praise I sent Eric (they trimmed it a bit, which often happens).

reviews.title: Must-read!
reviews.text: This book is an antidote to late-stage capitalism. It explains in direct language exactly how encrapification happens, and reveals the fascinatin mechanisms (which I once thought boring) that I can use as a founder and business advisor to drive real change.

reviews.title: A Thoughtful and Convincing Case That Mission Drift Is Not the Inevitable Price of Success
reviews.text:
This is one of the most thought-provoking business books I've read in years and one I'll be recommending far and wide.

Years ago, The Lean Startup was transformational for me as an entrepreneur and fundamentally changed how products and companies get built. Incorruptible feels equally ambitious, but aimed at an even bigger question...do organizations inevitably lose their mission as they scale or succeed?

I was fortunate to receive an advance copy and found it deeply inspiring.

What impressed me most is that this book does not stop at philosophy. It is deeply researched, highly informative, and packed with thoughtful real-world examples. Eric goes deep and builds a compelling case rather than simply offering a pie in the sky idea.

At its core, the book argues that corruption is not an inevitable byproduct of growth and that purpose and performance are not opposing forces. In fact, when done right, they reinforce one another. One of the most powerful ideas in the book is its challenge to the assumption that compromise and mission drift are simply the price of success.

As someone who teaches a class at Northwestern University on purpose in business and helps lead a mission-driven company, this one really hit home.

If Incorruptible has even a fraction of the impact that The Lean Startup had, I genuinely believe the world will be a better place.

Highly highly recommended!

reviews.title: Essential reading - how to defend against the rot eating us all
reviews.text:
We all know the feeling. Cory Doctorow recently immortalized it as 'encrapification'. It's when a product or platform that used to be so useful, so helpful, so good to us seems to turn, becoming adversarial, hostile, extractive. It serves more ads, requires more data, treats us as means and not ends. It's not necessarily that the platforms weren't making money before. But they apparently felt they weren't making enough - or growing enough. Doctorow is absolutely right in his description of the dynamic: first for users, then for business customers, then for investors. But he - and most all of us - tend to leave things there. After all, what more is there to say? As regrettable as it is, business exist for the benefit of their investors. That's just the way things are. We can break them up, regulate them, encourage competition, avoid them (to the extent we can) or hack workarounds. (All techniques that Doctorow describes in his own book.) But what we can't do is change the laws of "financial gravity" (as Ries calls it).

Or, can we? This is where Incorruptible comes in. It recognizes that in many cases, many, or even most, of the employees know full well when they are 'encrapifying' - or to use Ries' terminology, being corrupted. And they don't like it. They often don't want to go along. Even some leadership may not want to. But investors demand it. We remain stuck at the level of financial law.

But what if there was a way to guard against it from the outset - from the very inception of the company? To state, protect, and defend its principles and its mission? Not to turn for-profits into non-profits, but to ensure that companies make their money by providing real value. Incorruptible details the many perfectly feasible ways that this is in fact, possible - providing many real examples and resources along the way. From mission-protecting umbrella organizations to Public Benefit charters and much more.

Incorruptible is that rare work that is practical and immediately useful while also being genuinely humane and wise. It has my highest possible recommendation no matter your professional role, including consumer or concerned citizen. In short: it doesn't have to be this way.

reviews.title: A book every values-based founder needs
reviews.text: If you're a founder building something you believe in from a values-driven place, this book is a must-read. It's a guide for building something prosperous and impactful without forsaking values and integrity.

reviews.title: More important than any other business advice
reviews.text: I'm trying not to be hyperbolic, but this book is probably more important and can have more impact than anything else a founder can learn.

reviews.title: Much to gain
reviews.text: A worthwhile and compelling read. If you don't think you have the time or it's not for you, give it a try. Even if you gain one or two insights here, you, your team, and your (current/future) company and all involved have so much to gain.

reviews.title: A rare leadership book that refuses to separate mission from execution.
reviews.text: Eric Ries challenges the idea that large organizations have to become slow, political, or disconnected from purpose. Incorruptible is ultimately about building systems where innovation, accountability, and human-centered leadership can coexist at scale. Especially relevant for leaders trying to transform legacy industries instead of simply managing decline.

reviews.title: A refreshing antidote to greed is good
reviews.text: While some business books are inspiring and many can be viewed as helpful, very few inspire hope. Yet this one does. And that alone makes it worth reading. Though not sruprisingly, there is much to learn too, especially if you are a founder who wants to protect your business from the inevitable pressures to "corrupt" your values as you grow.

reviews.title: The only business book you'd be happy reading at the beach!
reviews.text: The other reviewers have done a great job capturing why this book is so vitally important, so I'll just add what a great read it is. That may seem surprising for a book on a serious topic, but Eric Ries is an *excellent* writer and storyteller. This would be an excellent gift for a full range of people you might be shopping for now: college graduation gift, fathers day, or just yourself.

reviews.title: Practical, knowledgeable and hopeful
reviews.text: Incorruptible has it all: Silicon Valley secrets, startup tips, examples of "well meaning" legal treachery, QR codes, superb writing, statistics and HOPE. Eric is not naive. He has been-there-done-that in all areas of  business. He proves that good business practice can be profitable. This book, and the community that has immediately united around it, are "powered by love".  Buy Incorruptible if you believe the world can be a better place.

reviews.title: More impact than Lean Startup for naming the problem and creating a playbook for 21st Century
reviews.text:
A decade ago, I stood on a TEDx stage talking about the "wacky world" of profit versus non-profit. I argued that the wall between "doing good" and "making money" was artificial. I was right about the why, but I didn't have the how. Later, I saw the consequences of that missing "how" firsthand at Rally Software. Despite our mission-driven culture and B-Corp status, when we hit the public markets, "Financial Gravity" took over. We found ourselves in a Crucible—a high-pressure environment where the system's default setting (short-term extraction) constantly fought our long-term vision. Without a new kind of structural power to resist, our mission was eventually deboned to satisfy the financial system. We were rolling back and forth in that crucible until the mission simply broke.

Eric Ries's new book, Incorruptible, is the manual I wish I had then. It provides the "how" for a transition that the business has been trying to make for decades.

In The Lean Startup, Eric Ries gave us a way to navigate uncertainty. It was brilliant for building products, but it didn't protect the company itself. You could build a "lean" team, but if it were housed inside a "corruptible" corporate structure, the system would eventually eat the innovation.

In Incorruptible, Ries scales his thinking from the product to the system. He realizes that you cannot solve a systemic problem with heroic leadership alone. He moves the focus from Heroism to Governance. Governance might sound boring, but I would argue this book is more important than Lean Startup, Good to Great, or Built to Last, at this moment in time.

Don't just build a great company. Build an Incorruptible one.
reviews.note: Rally Software founder (B Corp that went public and lost mission) — strong real-world cautionary tale

reviews.title: Well-written, a page turner, so inspiring
reviews.text: This book is a much needed idealism-restorative for our times--and it's well-written and absolutely compelling at every turn.

reviews.title: A book that will start a new movement
reviews.text:
Most business books describe problems we already know we have.

The good ones name something we've been living inside but couldn't articulate.

I got early access to Eric Ries's Incorruptible and read the whole thing in a weekend. Not because it's a page-turner, but because every few pages I found myself thinking "that's exactly what happened to that client" or "that's what's happening to us right now."

Fifteen years ago The Lean Startup started a movement. It gave a generation of product builders a shared language and a way to work. Incorruptible feels like that moment again, except this time Eric is taking on something bigger. Not how we build companies. Why they stop being worth building.

The concept of financial gravity alone is worth the read. The slow, structural pull that bends mission-driven organizations away from what they set out to do, not because of bad people, but because of how they were built. I've watched this happen up close more times than I want to admit. Never had a name for it until now.

MVP and pivot became core startup vocabulary because they named something real. Financial gravity, too early/too late, spiritual holding companies are doing the same.

Most founders will read this after the window has already started closing. Read it earlier than you think you need to.

reviews.title: Now IS the time for this.
reviews.text:
Incredibly important and timely.
Thank you Eric!

reviews.title: Building a better company
reviews.text: Interesting stories and a lot of good ideas about what it takes to survive in a shareholder profit driven world.

reviews.title: Financial gravity is the right name for it
reviews.text:
We have spent decades watching public institutions wither and corporations be co-opted by a small number of people optimizing for short-term profit. We became spectators. Our grandparents handed us a great deal, and we have not kept it running. Incorruptible is a serious answer to the question of how we start.

The book names a force that quietly destroys most of what we love about the companies that shaped our lives. Eric Ries calls it "financial gravity," and the framing is right. It is the structural pull of capital toward extraction, indifferent to the values of any individual founder or CEO. The book's argument is that good intentions are not a defense. Architecture is. Ries lays out, with unusual clarity, exactly what that architecture looks like and why it is buildable by anyone willing to do the work early enough.

The book's most important insight, for me, is its answer to when. There is never a good time to make your company incorruptible. The lawyers say wait, the VCs say wait, the bankers say wait, and then it is too late. Ries argues, correctly, that the moment to begin is now, wherever you are in your company's life. The work compounds. The longer you wait, the harder it becomes. As a founder who has done some of this work, I can confirm the rigor of the framework holds up in practice, not just on the page.

Read this if you have grown cynical about whether companies can be built differently. Read it if you suspect they can but don't know how. Read it especially if you are early enough in your own work that the architecture is still possible to build. The same dynamic that built the problem runs both ways. A small number of people, acting deliberately, can build the structures that protect what matters. Ries has written the manual we needed. The rest is up to us.
reviews.note: Highest helpful_count in snapshot (16). James Birchler already has multiple entries; the Amazon review itself is unshipped but covers similar ground.

reviews.title: Book about protecting the soul of our business
reviews.text:
Incorruptible, by Eric, is a book about how to structure a business with a moral compass. In the world of AI, every job is a startup, and everyone dreams of building a new company. This is exactly why this book matters now! When I built my startup, I signed all the documents lawyers gave me because I was told it was best practice?! Did I know that the corporate charter I signed obligated me to sell to the highest bidder, even if it were to be a cigarette company or a predatory acquirer that would fire all my founding colleagues??? There are many cautionary tales where Eric insists that we should be careful about taking the default path.

But this is also a book full of hope and inspiration, coupled with tactical and strategic tips and structures on how entrepreneurs and founders can keep their morals and visions aligned. Eric gives concrete examples such as Novo Nordisk, which is majority-owned by a foundation that protects its mission and has allowed the company to endure for over a hundred years. I don't think I even knew (or was offered) these structures when I started a company. If you're about to incorporate, or wish you'd thought harder when you did, make sure you have the important parts of the book underlined and re-read before you sign any legal papers. Darn, it was eye-opening, and inspiring. And if you don't plan to incorporate, get it anyways because it opens your eyes to the wonderful world of business structures, sorry to repeat, with a moral compass.

reviews.title: It can be better
reviews.text: When products are dehumanizing it is tempting to dismiss it as a product of the natural way that companies. But so often it is the result of deliberate choices that don't have to be made. This book makes the choices and their results clear.

reviews.title: How to protect a mission for your company
reviews.text:
When I read Ries's first book (Lean Startup) I loved the concept but felt the terms he crafted (Lean Startup and Minimal Viable Product) were too easy to misinterpret. That turned out to be true. But this time he has done it well. He uses the term FINANCIAL GRAVITY to refer to the force that causes companies, investors, boards, and others to work for short term financial returns at the expense of longer term goals (both financial and otherwise). Even when all the parties involved say they prefer the long term goals.

With many case studies and practical examples, Ries shows how firms can use corporate structure and other techniques to not only avoid this fate, but also improve financial returns while focusing on missions and other non-monetary goals.

Highly recommended for founders, CEOs, investors, board members and anyone who wants to push back against the idea that a company's only purpose is to serve its shareholders in the short term.

reviews.title: A wonderful book
reviews.text: This is an outstanding book that points the way forward to corporate America and to the start up community in particular. It provides tested means for companies to remain true to purpose and avoid the corruption of it that would otherwise ensue. The book is well written, highly informative and transformative. A book whose time has come. I got it on audio which was a particular joy.
reviews.note: Possibly Steen Thomsen, professor at Copenhagen Business School and a world expert on industrial foundations / steward ownership — verify before crediting

reviews.title: Beyond Shareholder Value
reviews.text:
I'm a huge fan of The Lean Startup, so when I picked up this book, I initially assumed it would not apply to me. Aren't all companies ultimately supposed to maximize returns for shareholders?

Eric challenged that assumption.

His introduction of concepts like the spiritual holding company and profit as the maximization of human flourishing fundamentally changed how I think about the role of business.

I have taught concepts from The Lean Startup for years and still believe those lessons are critical to building successful companies. But this book expands the conversation beyond efficiency and growth into something more foundational.

Building an incorruptible organization from the beginning is not a nice-to-have. It may be one of the most important decisions a founder makes.

This book gave me a new lens for evaluating not just how companies grow, but why they exist in the first place.

reviews.title: Very much worth reading
reviews.text: I really liked this book. The matter of sticking to your mission in the face of so much external pressure is amazing.

reviews.title: Must read
reviews.text: Incorruptible was delivered yesterday , and I picked it up and can't put it down.

reviews.title: Guidance for mission driven startups
reviews.text: Just like I wish I had Lean Startup 10 years earlier than it had come out, I wish I had this book 10 years earlier. A playbook for ensuring your company stays on mission.

reviews.title: Discover how not to destroy company trust & value over time
reviews.text: Investors including VCs and PE firms, board members, and startup founders should read this book. Many founders desire to build a mission-based firm, and employees want to work in one. The book explains the pressures that pull organizations away from their original purpose, to the long-term detriment of the firm. Ries explains how to preserve that trust and mission long-term without succumbing to prioritizing short-term value extraction that ultimately destroys the value of the firm.

reviews.title: Corruptibility Isn't a Moral Issue — It's a Structural One
reviews.text:
I thoroughly enjoyed and recommend Incorruptible to anyone starting or building a business. The stories alone are an amazing glimpse into the history of corporate governance, and show how structures and incentives can lead to corruptible or incorruptible companies.

To me, people create companies to achieve something no single person can, but that also means they need stronger protection from drift, attacks, and corruption. Eric Ries does an amazing job showing that this is not just a morality issue: being incorruptible can be achieved through practical governance structures. This book makes that idea feel practical, timely, and optimistic, especially in an age where trust in companies is so low.

reviews.title: Corruption has met its match!
reviews.text: Eric always has deep insight, and in this book, he really goes deep into an area we don't want to admit is happening, but we know it absolutely does. By defining corruption and talking about the consequences, he calls out the perpetrators in a way where everyone will know it when they see it. This will make it harder for those with guile to sneak by. He does a great job of shining the light on the darkness, and that is something this world is in desperate need of.

reviews.title: Must read for founders in 2026
reviews.text: If you are a founder wanting to build a generational company, this is a must read!

reviews.title: An inspiring book to help everyone challenge some of our oldest assumptions about companies
reviews.text:
I think this will quickly become recognized as a must-read for anyone who is involved in building or financing new businesses.

Through many case studies, Eric makes the business case for mission-driven organizations and then explains why many organizations that start out with a clear mission succumb to outside forces. Most importantly, he provides clear and actionable steps that anyone can take to ensure their organization will stay true to its mission over the long run.

I'm very interested to see how this book may shift the narrative on business structure and financing terms for start-ups in the years to come. Entrepreneurs are told to use standard terms to make financing as easy as possible but are the current standard terms actually serving the ecosystem as well as they could be?

Overall, I think this is an important book that will help to bring in a new generation of companies that stay great for the long haul.

reviews.title: A book that looks at real value
reviews.text: An incredible book that really meets the moment. The focus is on building incorruptible organizations and there is a part about the book being for people who want to be builders of new value in the world, not just move money around. That really spoke to me - and I appreciate Ries for adding this perspective on value to a business world that can often be focused on profit/money as the only measure of success.

reviews.title: The next question after Lean Startup
reviews.text: Eric came to Kiva years ago to dive into how we could accelerate our impact with Lean Startup, and as a nonprofit, we knew these first principles were more, not less, important to our execution and impact. Incorruptible takes on the next question: why good companies drift, and what structural choices around ownership, governance, and incentives matter. He treats those as design problems, not compliance ones. I found this to be my kind of page turner, making the case with examples from John Lewis, Patagonia, Vanguard, Anthropic. As someone working in employee ownership, I appreciate the clear thinking about what holds up over time and bringing broad-based employee ownership to the mainstream.

reviews.title: Read this to get the blueprint
reviews.text: I'm one year into my startup, and I already feel Financial Gravity pulling at decisions I didn't expect this early. Eric Ries doesn't just name that pull, he gives you the blueprint to design against it. I'm rethinking our governance, our cap table, our incentives, all of it, while we're still small enough to actually change them. Read this before you even start if you can. Easiest five stars I've ever given for a business book.

reviews.title: Costco hot dog is still $1.50
reviews.text: This book answered a question I didn't know I had: how is that hot dog and soda still a buck fifty? Eric Ries explains that companies like Costco aren't cheap by accident, they're designed to resist the pull toward cutting corners and squeezing you. Read it and you'll never look at your Costco membership the same way.
reviews.note: Consumer-perspective angle with strong helpful count

reviews.title: The book that changed how I'll pick my first job
reviews.text: Eric Ries put words to so much of what's felt frustrating and confusing about how business and capitalism actually work. I'm Gen Z, just graduated from college. Now I know how to weigh the opportunities in front of me by a company's corruptibility, not just the salary and the hours. This book should've come with my diploma.

reviews.title: The blueprint I wish I'd had decades ago
reviews.text: I've been in mission-oriented tech startups for three decades and I've watched the same movie so many times: a company with real soul gets acquired, optimized, and surgically deboned until nothing's left but the logo. I'd unconsciously accepted it. Eric Ries names the force behind the decay, "Financial Gravity," and then shows the rare companies engineered to resist it. Even better, for practical leaders like me, he offers a blueprint on what to do, even what to say to your lawyer. (For the academic types, lots of research citied and a gazillion pages of end notes.) Highly recommend for teams to read together.

reviews.title: How a focus on caring and listening helps companies of all sizes.
reviews.text:
I have read other books by the author.
And have seen his talk about this book in person.
He is a top thinker.

He helps us see companies that have a large vision. And that both care for the investors, but always keep the whole world in mind. A select few have done this very well for a hundred years. And it grows each year. And is much needed.

Can we be kinder to each other? Here is a good argument for the strong need and the strong practicality of asking such questions.

reviews.title: Eric Ries does it again
reviews.text: Great book, Ries is an OG when it comes to startups, and this book was a great retrospective on how companies scale without losing their 'soul'
